A system of linear inequalities is useful in solving applications with two quantities limited by two or more constraints. For example, a retail store may have a restriction to spend no more than a certain amount to stock some new products. Writing an inequality to represent this situation will give a set of solutions representing the amounts of the new product which will work within the given restriction. If the retail store has an additional constraint regarding these new products, such as a minimum profit made, a second inequality can be written. Together these two inequalities form a system of inequalities.
When solving these application problems, consider the same steps we use to solve an application which uses a system of linear equations.
Select two different variables to represent two unknown quantities.
Form two or more inequalities involving each of the variables. The phrases in the table below may help you determine which inequality sign is appropriate.
To earn a grade of A, you must score at least 90%.
The perimeter is at most 75 feet.
The perimeter is less than 30 feet.
The perimeter is no less than 100 centimeters.
The area is more than 30 square inches.
The area is no more than 100 square yards.
The car's speed exceeded the limit of 45 mph.
The altitude is between 10,000 and 15,000 feet.

Recall that to solve a system of linear inequalities in two variables, we graph each inequality on the same coordinate axes, and then find the region where the graphs overlap. For most of these application problems, we will only want to consider nonnegative values for the variables, and therefore only use the part of the graph that lies in the first quadrant.

A homeowner budgets from $300 to $600 for trees and shrubs to landscape their yard. After shopping around, they find that good trees cost $150 and mature shrubs cost $75. What combinations of trees and shrubs can the homeowner afford to buy?
We know that each tree costs $150 and each shrub costs $75.
We also know that the homeowner wants to spend at least $300 but no more than $600 for the plants.
We need to determine what combinations of trees and shrubs will meet the requirements.

Together, the two inequalities defined a set of solutions that meet the restrictions on the amount the homeowner is willing to spend. Since the homeowner cannot buy a part of a tree or a part of a shrub, we used dots to mark the distinct pairs of trees and shrubs.

The ordered pairs (0, 4), (0, 5), (0, 6), (0, 7), and (0, 8) show that if no trees are purchased, then 4 to 8 shrubs can be purchased.
The ordered pairs (1, 2), (1, 3), (1, 4), (1, 5), and (1, 6) show that if 1 tree is purchased, then 2 to 6 shrubs can be purchased.
The ordered pairs (2, 0), (2, 1), (2, 2), (2, 3), and (2, 4) show that if 2 trees are purchased then 0 to 4 shrubs can be purchased.
The ordered pairs (3, 0), (3, 1), and (3, 2) show that if 3 trees are purchased then 0 to 2 shrubs can be purchased.
Lastly, the ordered pair (4, 0) shows that if 4 trees are purchased then no shrubs can be purchased.
